intro.title: Leverage in your account
intro.summary: Before your first trade: how much each lot puts at stake in a {start} account with 1:{leverage} leverage.

s1.title: One pip, how many dollars?
s1.p1: In this account, 1 lot = {contract} units of currency. On {pair}, {bigLot} lot makes each pip worth {bigPip}. With {smallLot} lot, one pip is only {smallPip}.
s1.p2: 1:{leverage} leverage means you only put up 1/{leverage} of the position's value as margin. The position is still big, so its gains and losses are big too.
s1.caption: {pair} at {price}, starting balance {start}. Disiplin limit: at most {maxRisk}% risk per trade.

s2.title: Why small lots first
s2.p1: A {lossPips}-pip loss on {bigLot} lot wipes out {bigLossPct} of your balance in one trade. With {smallLot} lot, the same loss is only {smallLossPct}.
s2.p2: The margin for {bigLot} lot ({bigMargin}) is already more than half of a {start} balance. That's why Stage 1 uses {smallLot} lot.

s3.title: Stop out
s3.p1: Margin level = equity ÷ margin in use. If it falls to {stopOut}%, every trade is closed automatically so your balance doesn't go negative. That's called a stop out.
s3.p2: Example: one {outLot}-lot trade uses {outMargin} of margin. Stop out happens when equity is down to {outEquity}, that is after a {outLoss} loss, or about {outPips} pips.

s4.title: When the account runs out
s4.p1: In Stage 1, if no trade is open and your balance is below {habis}, your account has run out and trading stops. The line is the same on every chart: the margin for {minLot} lot on your stage's most expensive pair, rounded up. Above it, the smallest trade always fits. The line is also shown on your account dashboard.
s4.p2: There's no button to add money. Rex reviews your account from its own data, you work through a short risk lesson, then you start a new account at the starting balance.

intro.question: You open {bigLot} lot of {pair} with a {lossPips}-pip stop loss. If the SL is hit, what percentage of the {start} starting balance do you lose?
intro.explain: Correct. {lossPips} pips × {bigPip} = {bigLoss}, and {bigLoss} ÷ {start} = {bigLossPct}. With {smallLot} lot, the loss is only {smallLoss} ({smallLossPct}).
intro.hint: Not yet. Look at the table: what is 1 pip worth for {bigLot} lot? Multiply by {lossPips}, then compare with {start}.

risk.title: Position size starts from risk
risk.summary: Before your next account: how to choose a lot size from your stop loss, so a single trade never takes more than {maxRisk}% of your balance.

s1.title: Start from a risk budget
s1.p1: The lot size isn't the first step. First decide how much you're willing to lose if your idea is wrong. The Disiplin limit here is {maxRisk}% of your balance: with a {start} balance, that's {budget} per trade.
s1.p2: That number stays the same however sure you feel about the setup. Only the lot size changes, following the distance to your stop loss.

s2.title: From stop loss to lot size
s2.p1: Loss at SL = (SL distance + spread) × pip value. On {pair}, {minLot} lot is worth {perPip} per pip and the spread is about {spread} pips, which you pay as soon as the trade opens.
s2.p2: Put your SL where your idea is proven wrong, then find the biggest lot whose loss still fits the budget. A wider SL means a smaller lot.
s2.caption: {pair} at {price}, spread {spread} pips, balance {start}, budget {budget} ({maxRisk}%). "None" rows: the loss figure uses {minLot} lot.

s3.title: When even the smallest lot is too big
s3.p1Far: With a {sl}-pip SL, {minLot} lot alone already loses {loss} ({lossPct}). Don't move your SL closer just to pass the limit: an SL that's too close gets hit by ordinary movement.
s3.p1: If even {minLot} lot goes over the limit, don't move your SL closer just to pass: an SL that's too close gets hit by ordinary movement.
s3.p2: Skip that setup and wait for a cleaner one. Not trading is a disciplined decision too.

s4.title: A loss doesn't need paying back
s4.p1: After a loss, your lot size still follows the budget, not the urge to win it back. A bigger lot within {window} candles of a loss counts as a revenge trade.
s4.p2: Your next account starts at the starting balance again. Your stage stays, and so does the old account's journal in Account history.

risk.question: Balance {start}, risk limit {maxRisk}%, SL {q} pips on {pair} (spread {spread} pips). What's the biggest lot that still passes the risk check?
risk.explain: Correct. Your budget is {budget}. With a {q}-pip SL plus a {spread}-pip spread, {answerLot} lot loses {atLoss} ({atPct}) at the SL. {overLot} lot already loses {overLoss} ({overPct}), over the limit.
risk.hint: Not yet. Work out your budget first ({maxRisk}% of {start}), then the loss per {minLot} lot: (SL + spread) × {perPip}. Don't forget the spread.

create.title: Create a Practice Account
create.body: You get a virtual balance of {balance} with 1:{leverage} leverage, then trade on historical charts that play out candle by candle. What's scored is your discipline, not your profit. If the balance runs out, there's no top-up: we review it together, then start a new account.

reset.confirmBody: Account #{n} will be closed and recorded as reset in Account history. Its balance isn't carried over. Rex reviews your account first, then you open Account #{next}.

tipsPage.title: Rex's Tips
tipsPage.body: Rex shows up once, right when something important happens. Tips you've already seen can be read again here.

limits.l1: Real money feels different. Losing a few dollars of a virtual balance doesn't make your heart race; money you need can.
limits.l2: Here you can pause a chart and play it candle by candle. Real markets keep moving, including while you sleep or you're busy.
limits.l3: Real execution can fill away from the price you see (slippage), and spreads can widen around big news.
limits.l4: Costs, leverage and rules differ from provider to provider, and all of them shape the result.
limits.l5: The charts here have already happened. Practice results don't predict real trading results.
